source_text: Perspecta igitur abysso impietatis tuae, licet numquam quidquam possit profanius inveniri; tamen quam hoc nihil habeat virium, et quid de illis quae annexueras colligatur, brevi disputatione monstrabitur. Deus qui hoc appellari nomine voluit, ut omnipotentissimus, ita etiam iustissimus creditur; quorum si unum defuerit, neutrum aderit; ut conditor benignissimus hominum, ita meritorum expunctor aequissimus; omne quod facit, bonum valde est [n318] . Ac per hoc, nemo naturaliter malus est, sed quicumque reus est, moribus, non exordiis accusatur.
pass_a_gloss: The abyss of your impiety therefore having been looked through, although never anything more profane can be found; nevertheless how this has nothing of strengths, and what is gathered from those things which you had annexed, will be shown by a brief disputation. God who willed to be called by this name, as most omnipotent, so also most just is believed; of which if one shall have been lacking, neither will be present; as most benign founder of humans, so most equitable settler of deserts; everything which he makes, is very good. And through this, no one is naturally evil, but whoever is guilty, is accused by manners, not by beginnings.

lemmas.lexica: LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS meritum=desert; Blaise without later merit-system

pass_b_english: Having surveyed the abyss of your impiety, though nothing more profane could ever be found, a brief discussion will nevertheless show how powerless it is and what follows from the things you added. God, who wished to be called by this name, is believed to be supremely just as well as supremely powerful. If one of these is absent, neither will be present. He is humanity's most kindly Creator and the most equitable assessor of what each deserves. Everything he makes is very good (Genesis 1:31). Consequently, no one is evil by nature; whoever is guilty is accused for conduct, not origins.

choices.why: Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

bible_refs.note: From Pass B Scripture tagging; wording follows Julian's Latin, not a modern Bible.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
